explanation: Analyte-resolved contaminant fate means that for each named contaminant, the mass in each output stream is reported so that the mass leaving the process can be compared with the mass entering it. A total contaminant number cannot do this job, and a single favourable removal figure for one analyte does not transfer to another.
title: Analyte-resolved contaminant fate
tooltip: Knowing where each named contaminant ends up, not just that the total is smaller.

assumptions: The six method families catalogued in Batch-02 represent the complete set of known recycling approaches for cigarette butts as of the retrieval window.
Heavy metals (cadmium, lead, arsenic, mercury) are correctly treated as a stop condition rather than a parameter to be traded off.
A mass balance that is not dry-mass-based and analyte-resolved cannot establish that contaminants have been removed rather than redistributed.
A product gate that depends on mass-balance closure is circular and does not protect the intended use.
No located source demonstrates analytical performance (inlet-to-outlet) for any contaminant in any of the six families.

auditReferences.label: Batch-02 Invention Sketch (Phase 2 — Prior-Art Awareness Only)

failureModes: A later pilot demonstrates that one or more method families can achieve dry-mass and analyte-resolved closure without meeting the four-field sink prerequisite, falsifying the necessity claim.
Heavy metals are shown to be consistently below background in all process streams for a family, making the stop condition moot for that family.
A jurisdiction accepts a recovered material based on total contaminant limits rather than analyte-resolved fate, making the analyte-resolved field unnecessary in that context.
A product gate is established that is independent of mass-balance closure and is met by a family without the four-field sink being fully satisfied.
The metals stop-condition cannot be analytically implemented at the required sensitivity, making the prerequisite infeasible.
falsifiers: Published pilot-scale data showing complete dry-mass balance with analyte-resolved contaminant fate for any of the six families.
Published analytical method validation demonstrating inlet-to-outlet performance for cadmium, lead, arsenic, and mercury across all process streams for any family.
A regulatory acceptance decision for a cigarette-butt-derived product that does not require analyte-resolved fate.
A demonstrated product-quality gate that is independent of mass-balance closure and is passed by a family without the four-field sink.
mechanism: This hypothesis proposes that the four-field sink (dry-mass balance on a common dry-feed basis, analyte-resolved contaminant fate across all output streams, a named final treatment route with a jurisdiction-specific acceptance basis, and a use-specific product gate independent of mass-balance closure) must be a mandatory prerequisite for any later authorized pilot. The metals stop-condition is in force: any detectable metal above background in feedstock, wash water, air emission, solid residue, or final product triggers a halt; the stream cannot resume until analytical performance (inlet-to-outlet) is demonstrated. This sketch does not propose how to remove metals; it proposes that metals are a stop condition, not a solvable parameter within this sketch. The six method families remain as unvalidated inputs to this prerequisite framework.
priorContext: Batch-01 identified cigarette butt recycling as an open problem with no located evidence of full-butt recycling at any scale. Six method families were catalogued (mechanical-physical, thermal, chemical, biological, material-incorporation, product-routes). Batch-01 established heavy metals as an explicit stop condition. Batch-02 reviewed all six families and found each fails at least one field of the four-field sink: dry-mass closure, analyte-resolved contaminant fate, use-specific product gate, and metals stop condition. No family demonstrates a complete dry-mass balance with analyte-resolved accounting; no family shows where each measured analyte goes through every process step; no family sets an independent product-quality gate separate from mass-balance closure; no family treats metals as an explicit stop condition with a demonstrated analytical test.

title: Batch-02 Invention Sketch: Four-Field Sink as Mandatory Pilot Prerequisite
unresolvedDependencies: Quantitative input-output data at pilot scale for any of the six method families.
Demonstrated analytical method performance for heavy metals across all process streams (inlet-to-outlet).
A use-specific product-quality standard for any recovered material from cigarette butts.
Novelty/patentability search — this sketch has NOT performed one.
Regulatory acceptance basis for any final route in any jurisdiction.

compositionSummary: A spent cigarette butt is a layered composite rather than a single material: a cellulose acetate filter tow, a paper wrapper carrying combustion residue, a short tobacco rod that retains tobacco-specific compounds, and fine ash. What matters for every recycling route is that these layers carry different contaminants, so a process that treats the butt as one material will either leave some contaminants untouched or redistribute them without removing them.

explanation: A dry-mass basis states the mass of material excluding water, so that a wet lot and a dried lot of the same material can be compared. Without it, two reported splits can describe the same material, and a balance cannot be checked. Several published figures for this material do not state whether they were measured wet or dry.
title: Dry-mass basis
tooltip: A way of counting mass that does not change with how wet the material is.

explanation: The four fields are a dry-mass balance on a common dry-feed basis, analyte-resolved contaminant fate across the streams, a named final treatment route with a jurisdiction-specific acceptance basis, and a use-specific product gate that is independent of whether the mass balance closes. A method family that cannot locate all four is a hypothesis with a measurement plan attached, not a finished route.
title: The four-field sink
tooltip: The four things that must be located before a recovered material can be called a product.

explanation: Heavy metals are treated throughout this layer as a stop condition rather than as a value to be averaged or traded off. A stream whose heavy-metal content has not been characterised cannot be routed to a product or to unclassified waste, and a favourable result on another criterion does not offset that.
title: Heavy metals

mechanism: Two variants sit in this family. In staged washing, butts are washed in water and then optionally in ethanol, and the filter material is recovered without being dissolved. In the grinding route, butts are milled so that the filter fraction separates from the paper and tobacco matrix, sieved out, washed in water, dried and milled again into fibrous particles. In both variants the question is the same: whether washing removes contaminants from the fibre or only redistributes them between fibre, water and sludge.
